a: Ignatius, also called Theophorus
p: The same second name opens every letter: Theophorus, 'God-bearer'.
b: Greek Theophoros, 'God-bearer'. Lake's footnote gives the story of the third-century Acts of Ignatius: asked 'And who is Theophorus?', Ignatius answers, 'He who has Christ in his heart.' Lightfoot notes that a later story, that Ignatius was the child Jesus took in his arms, was 'built upon a misinterpretation of Θεοφόρος'. See the note at Ignatius to the Romans 1:0.

a: lacks no gift
p: Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 1:7, Paul's praise of the Corinthians.
b: Greek anysterētō ousē pantos charismatos, 'falling short in no gift'. Paul told the Corinthians, 'So you are not lacking in any gift as you eagerly wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ' (1 Corinthians 1:7). The 'gift' (charisma) is the word for the Spirit's gifts in 1 Corinthians 12.

a: a bearer of holy things
p: Greek hagiophoros, one of Ignatius's '-bearer' words, like Theophorus.
b: Greek hagiophoros. Ignatius calls the Ephesians 'God-bearers and temple-bearers, Christ-bearers, bearers of holy things' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:2); here the whole church is one. The picture is of a procession carrying sacred objects. Lake: 'gifted with holiness'.

a: Smyrna, in Asia
p: A port city of the Roman province of Asia, one of the seven churches of Revelation.
b: The risen Christ's letter to 'the angel of the church in Smyrna' promises 'the crown of life' to those faithful to death (Revelation 2:8-11). Ignatius had stayed there on his way to Rome; Eusebius says he wrote four letters at Smyrna, 'where Polycarp was', and then wrote 'from Troas ... to the church of Smyrna; and particularly to Polycarp, who presided over the latter church' (Church History 3.36.5, 10). This letter never names Polycarp; it greets 'your overseer, worthy of God' (12:2).
orig: τῇ οὔσῃ ἐν Σμύρνῃ τῆς Ἀσίας

a: Jesus Christ, the God who has made you so wise
p: Ignatius opens the body of the letter by giving glory to Jesus Christ as God.
b: Greek Iēsoun Christon ton theon ton houtōs hymas sophisanta, 'Jesus Christ, the God who thus made you wise'. Lake: 'Jesus Christ, the God who has thus given you wisdom'. Ignatius calls Christ God in every letter (see the note at Ignatius to the Romans 1:0) and in the next lines insists just as hard that he was truly human. The two belong together for him: the one who suffered in the flesh is God (compare 'the suffering of my God', Ignatius to the Romans 6:3).

a: He is truly of David's family
p: 1:1-2 reads like an early statement of faith: David's line, Son of God, born of a virgin, baptized, nailed under Pilate.
b:
The lines are built on the word 'truly' (alēthōs), set against those who said it all only seemed to happen (2:1). Lake's margin gives Romans 1:3, and Lightfoot says Ignatius 'doubtless had in his mind' that verse, where Jesus 'according to the flesh, came from the offspring of David' and was marked out as Son of God 'in power' (Romans 1:3-4). Then come the birth from a virgin (Matthew 1:23; Luke 1:34-35), the baptism by John (Matthew 3:13-17), the crucifixion under Pontius Pilate and Herod (Luke 23:6-12; Acts 4:27), and the resurrection (1:2; 2:1).

Lightfoot compares a similar 'truly' in To the Trallians 9 ('who was truly born'). The letter does not say whether Ignatius is quoting a fixed formula or putting the church's teaching in his own words.
r: Romans 1:3-4; Matthew 1:23; Matthew 3:13-17; Luke 23:6-12; Acts 4:27; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; 1 Timothy 3:16

a: truly born of a virgin
p: Ignatius repeats 'truly' five times in a few lines.
b: Greek alēthōs, 'truly, really': 'truly of David's family', 'truly born', 'truly nailed' (1:2), 'truly suffered ... truly raised himself' (2:1). The Plain English Translation keeps every one, because the repetition is the argument: each fact of Christ's life happened in a real body. 'Born' renders gegennēmenon, which Lightfoot says 'we must certainly read with Theodoret'; his Greek manuscript G has gegenēmenon, 'come into being' (see the variant). On the birth see the topic page.

a: so that by him all righteousness might be fulfilled
p: Ignatius gives the reason for Jesus's baptism found only in Matthew.
b: Greek hina plērōthē pasa dikaiosynē hyp' autou. Lake's margin gives Matthew 3:15, where Jesus tells John, 'Doing it this way is fitting for us, to fulfill all righteousness' (Matthew 3:15). Ignatius has the passive, 'that all righteousness might be fulfilled by him', so the Plain English Translation translates his words. Lightfoot: 'Nothing is said respecting the motive of Jesus in coming to baptism in the other Canonical Gospels.' This is one of the signs that Ignatius knew Matthew's Gospel or its tradition.
orig: ἵνα πληρωθῇ πᾶσα δικαιοσύνη ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ

a: Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch
p: Ignatius names both rulers, as Luke and Acts do.
b: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea; 'Herod the tetrarch' is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, whom Luke calls tetrarch (Luke 3:1) and to whom Pilate sent Jesus (Luke 23:7). The church's prayer in Acts names the two together: 'Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with Gentiles and the peoples of Israel' (Acts 4:27). Naming the officials fixes the crucifixion in public history against those who made it an appearance.
orig: ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου καὶ Ἡρώδου τετράρχου

a: We are from that fruit
p: Ignatius pictures the cross as a tree and the church as its fruit.
b: Greek aph' hou karpou hēmeis, 'from which fruit we are'. Lake's footnote: '"Tree" is not expressed in the Greek: but seems to be implied by the "fruit" in the next sentence, though the exact meaning of the passage is obscure.' The church grows from the cross, as fruit from a tree (compare Acts 5:30, 'hanging him on a tree'). Lake marks the clause as a parenthesis.

a: raise a flag for all ages
p: Lake's margin gives Isaiah's 'he will raise a flag for faraway nations'.
b: Greek hina arē syssēmon, 'that he might raise a signal'. The Greek Isaiah 5:26 has the same words, arei syssēmon, where the site's Isaiah, from the Hebrew, reads 'He will raise a flag for faraway nations' (Isaiah 5:26); Lake's margin adds Isaiah 11:12, 49:22 and 62:10. Lightfoot: 'Ignatius sees the fulfilment of this in Christ's resurrection. Hence the words' about Jews and nations that follow. He also suggests the 'standard' may be in John 12:32, 'when I am lifted up'. Ephesians 2:16 (in Lake's margin) gives 'one body'.
orig: ἵνα ἄρῃ σύσσημον εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας
r: Isaiah 5:26; Isaiah 11:12; Isaiah 49:22; Isaiah 62:10; John 12:32; Ephesians 2:16

a: he suffered only in appearance
p: Greek to dokein, 'the seeming': the word behind the name docetism.
b:
Greek to dokein auton peponthenai, 'that he suffered in seeming'. Dokein means 'to seem'; from it comes 'docetism', the name later given to the belief that Christ's body, or his suffering, was only an appearance. Lake's introduction: Ignatius 'protests against the form of heresy called docetism (δοκεῖν), which regarded the sufferings, and in some cases the life, of Jesus as merely an appearance'.

Ignatius turns the word on the teachers: 'They themselves are only in appearance!' Their faith is a show, and so will their end be: 'bodiless, like demons'. Lake's footnote at the first 'only in appearance' of 4:2 says that 'here and elsewhere' the Berlin papyrus and the long recension read the dative tō dokein against the accusative to dokein of the Greek manuscript G (see the variant at 4:2); the sense is the same. The papyrus begins at 3:3, so at 2:1 the footnote's 'elsewhere' can apply only to the long recension.
orig: τὸ δοκεῖν αὐτὸν πεπονθέναι, αὐτοὶ τὸ δοκεῖν ὄντες

a: he also truly raised himself
p: Ignatius says Christ raised himself; in 7:1 the Father raised him.
b: Greek anestēsen heauton, 'raised himself'. The New Testament usually says God raised him (Acts 2:24; Romans 10:9), as Ignatius himself does at 7:1 ('which the Father raised'). In John's Gospel Jesus says 'I have the right to lay it down, and I have the right to take it back again' (John 10:18) and 'within three days I will raise it' (John 2:19). Ignatius holds both without explaining.

a: he was in the flesh even after the resurrection
p: Ignatius insists the risen Christ had flesh, the point Luke 24 makes.
b:
The risen Jesus in Luke says 'a spirit has no flesh and bones, and you can see that I have them' (Luke 24:39), and eats fish before the disciples (Luke 24:42-43). Paul calls the resurrection body a 'spiritual body' (1 Corinthians 15:44). Ignatius holds both: Christ ate and drank 'as a man of flesh, though in spirit he was united with the Father' (3:3).

Lightfoot notes that Jerome and the Latin version read 'I saw him in the flesh', as if Ignatius had seen the risen Lord; the Greek says 'I know'. Eusebius quotes 'I know and believe that he was in the flesh after the resurrection' (Church History 3.36.11, New Advent English).
orig: μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν ἐν σαρκὶ αὐτὸν οἶδα

a: I am not a bodiless demon
p: A saying of the risen Jesus close to Luke 24:39 in sense, but in other words. Its source was already a puzzle in the 300s.
b:
Greek ouk eimi daimonion asōmaton. The site's Luke 24:39 reads: 'Feel me and look: a spirit has no flesh and bones, and you can see that I have them' (Luke 24:39). Lake's margin says only 'Cf. Luke 24, 39'. 'Demon' renders daimonion as elsewhere on the site; here it means a disembodied spirit or ghost.

Where did the words come from? Eusebius quotes them and says Ignatius took them 'I know not whence' (Church History 3.36.11). Jerome says the saying is in 'the Gospel which I have recently translated' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16), the Gospel according to the Hebrews, as Lightfoot shows from Jerome's other works. Origen, as Lightfoot quotes him, found 'I am not a bodiless demon' in a book 'called the Teaching of Peter', which he says 'is not held among the church's books' (On First Principles, preface 8). Lightfoot: 'it is impossible to say whether he got it from oral tradition or from some written source'. See the topic on sayings of Jesus outside the Gospels.
orig: Λάβετε, ψηλαφήσατέ με καὶ ἴδετε, ὅτι οὐκ εἰμὶ δαιμόνιον ἀσώματον

a: those with Peter
p: Greek hoi peri Petron: Peter and the others with him.
b: Lightfoot: the phrase means 'the Eleven and those with them', as in Luke 24:33-34; 'the plurals following ... are decisive' that more than Peter is meant. He adds that Zahn compared the short ending added to Mark in some manuscripts, which uses the same phrase.

a: joined to his flesh
p: The verb means 'mixed, blended': by touching him they were joined to him.
b: Greek krathentes tē sarki autou kai tō pneumati, from kerannymi, 'mix'. Lake: 'being mingled both with his flesh and spirit'. The Armenian reads 'blood' for 'spirit' (see the variant). Lightfoot gives the Armenian in Latin: 'they believed who shared in the eucharist and supped before on his body and blood'. He says: 'The first clause is evidently a gloss (prob. later and certainly erroneous) of the second; and the rendering generally points to κραθέντες.'
orig: κραθέντες τῇ σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ τῷ πνεύματι

a: he ate and drank with them
p: Lake's margin gives Acts 10:41.
b: Greek synephagen autois kai synepien, 'he ate with them and drank with them'. Peter tells Cornelius: 'We shared meals with him, eating and drinking, after he rose from among the dead' (Acts 10:41), the same pair of verbs. Luke 24:43 has him eat 'with them watching'.

a: beasts in human form
p: Ignatius, going to the beasts, calls the false teachers beasts that look like men.
b: Greek tōn thēriōn tōn anthrōpomorphōn. The Catholic Encyclopedia's article on the Docetae quotes it as 'monsters in human shape'. The picture is sharp from a man who will face real beasts in Rome (4:2; Ignatius to the Romans 4:1). Yet he tells the church to pray for them, 'in case they may somehow repent', and says Christ has power to bring that about. Compare Paul's 'fierce wolves' (Acts 20:29).

a: then I too am in chains only in appearance
t: If his suffering was a show, so are my chains
p: Ignatius's argument from his own suffering: a seeming Christ makes a real martyr a fool.
b: Ignatius argues from his own chains: if Christ only seemed to suffer, then Ignatius's suffering for him is pointless: 'why have I handed myself over to death?' The same argument stands in his letter To the Trallians (chapter 10), which the Catholic Encyclopedia quotes: 'Then I die for nothing.' Paul argues the same way about the resurrection: 'And we ourselves, why are we in danger every hour?' (1 Corinthians 15:30).

a: near the sword is near God
p: Two short sayings: near the sword is near God; among beasts is among God.
b: Greek engys machairas engys theou, metaxy thēriōn metaxy theou. The sayings have the ring of a proverb, and they turn the means of execution, the sword and the beasts, into the place of God's nearness. Lake: 'near the sword is near to God, with the wild beasts is with God'. See Ignatius to the Romans 4:1-2.
orig: ἐγγὺς μαχαίρας ἐγγὺς θεοῦ, μεταξὺ θηρίων μεταξὺ θεοῦ

a: the perfect human being, makes me strong
p: Christ is 'the perfect man', and he strengthens Ignatius, as Philippians 4:13.
b: Greek autou me endynamountos tou teleiou anthrōpou. Lake's margin gives Philippians 4:13, 'I have strength for everything in the one who makes me strong' (Philippians 4:13), the same verb. Christ as 'the perfect human being' is the answer to the teachers who denied his humanity: he is not less than human but the complete human (compare 'the new man', Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:1). The Greek manuscript and the Latin add 'who became' (see the variant).
orig: αὐτοῦ με ἐνδυναμοῦντος τοῦ τελείου ἀνθρώπου

a: they have been denied by him
p: Those who deny him have been denied by him, as Jesus warned.
b: Greek ērnēthēsan hyp' autou. Jesus: 'whoever denies me in front of people, I too will deny that person in front of my Father in heaven' (Matthew 10:33; compare 2 Timothy 2:12). The 'prophecies', 'the law of Moses' and 'the gospel' are the three witnesses Ignatius appeals to (compare 7:2), with the martyrs' own sufferings as a fourth.

a: flesh-bearing
p: Two coined words: Christ 'bore flesh'; whoever denies it 'bears a corpse'.
b: Greek sarkophoron, 'flesh-bearing', and nekrophoros, 'corpse-bearing', built like 'Theophorus'. Lake: 'clothed in flesh' and 'clothed with a corpse'. To deny Christ's flesh is to carry death around in one's own body. The confession required is John's: 'Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh' (1 John 4:2).

a: I have not thought it right to write them down
p: Ignatius refuses to name the false teachers.
b: He will not even remember them 'until they repent'. The letter therefore gives no names, and who exactly they were is unknown. Lake says it 'is disputed' whether the Judaizing tendency Ignatius attacks in other letters belonged to the same circles as the docetism attacked here. Compare 3 John 9-10, where the Elder names Diotrephes.

a: the suffering, which is our resurrection
p: Greek pathos, 'suffering', the word behind 'the Passion'.
b: Greek to pathos, ho estin hēmōn anastasis. Christ's suffering is 'our resurrection' because his real death and rising are the ground of ours (1 Corinthians 15:20-22). To deny the one is to lose the other.
orig: εἰς τὸ πάθος, ὅ ἐστιν ἡμῶν ἀνάστασις

a: the glory of the angels, and the rulers seen and unseen
p: Even heavenly powers face judgment if they do not believe in Christ's blood.
b: Greek hoi archontes horatoi te kai aoratoi, 'the rulers, visible and invisible', the language of Colossians 1:16, where all things were created in Christ, 'the seen and the unseen' (Colossians 1:16). Lightfoot paraphrases: 'Even the angels will be judged, if they believe not in Christ's blood.' Paul: 'Do you not know that we will judge angels' (1 Corinthians 6:3). Ignatius's point: no rank in heaven or on earth is above faith in the cross, so 'Let no one's place puff him up.'
orig: καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες ὁρατοί τε καὶ ἀόρατοι

a: Let the one who makes room for this make room for it
t: 'Let the one who can receive it'
p: A saying of Jesus from Matthew 19:12, in Lake's margin.
b: Greek ho chōrōn chōreitō, 'the one making room, let him make room'. Matthew 19:12 has ho dynamenos chōrein chōreitō: 'Let anyone who can make room for this make room for it' (Matthew 19:12). Ignatius drops 'can'; the Plain English Translation keeps the site's verb. In Matthew it closes the saying on eunuchs for the kingdom; Ignatius uses it as a general call to accept a hard truth.

a: hold other opinions
p: Greek heterodoxeo, the verb behind English 'heterodox'.
b: Greek tous heterodoxountas, 'those who hold other opinions', from heteros, 'other', and doxa, 'opinion'. It is the opposite of 'orthodox', 'right opinion'. Lake: 'those who have strange opinions'. Paul uses the cousin word heterodidaskaleō, 'teach otherwise' (1 Timothy 1:3).

a: They do not care about love
p: Ignatius ties the false teaching to neglect of the poor: no care for widow, orphan, prisoner or hungry.
b:
The list is the Bible's list of people God defends: the widow and the orphan (Exodus 22:22; James 1:27), the oppressed, the prisoner, the hungry and thirsty (Matthew 25:35-36). Lightfoot: 'The first care of the Church was to provide for the wants of the widows'. Ignatius's charge is that a faith that denies Christ's body also neglects bodies: those who make the flesh unreal do not feed it.

Whether this is a fair description of the opponents cannot be checked, since no writing of theirs survives. Ignatius's point is that right belief and love belong together, as in 1 John 3:17-18 and 4:20.

a: the thanksgiving
p: Greek eucharistia, the word that became 'Eucharist'. Here it plainly names the church's meal.
b: Greek eucharistia, 'thanksgiving', the word that became 'Eucharist'. The Plain English Translation keeps 'the thanksgiving', as in the Didache and in Ignatius's other letters, so the reader sees one Greek word throughout; the churches call the rite the Eucharist, the Lord's Supper, Holy Communion or the Divine Liturgy. The first eucharistias in the verse has no article, so on its own it could mean thanksgiving in general; the second clause shows that the rite is meant. Here the word names the rite itself, and even the bread: 'the thanksgiving is the flesh of our Savior'. Lake translates 'Eucharist'. The Catholic Encyclopedia says that in Ignatius 'we find for the first time' the word 'applied to the Blessed Sacrament' (it gives Smyrnaeans 8); the Didache also uses it of the meal (Didache 9:1).

a: the thanksgiving is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ
t: 'The flesh of our Savior': how the churches read 7:1
p: Lightfoot reads it as an argument about Christ's flesh; Catholic and Lutheran writers, as his presence in the Supper.
b:
Ignatius says the teachers stay away 'because they do not confess that the thanksgiving is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, which suffered ... and which the Father raised'. Lightfoot explains the logic: like Tertullian against Marcion, 'The eucharist implies the reality of Christ's flesh. To those who deny this reality, it has no meaning at all.' He also infers from 8:1 that they held 'a eucharist of their own apart from the Church'.

Catholic: Joseph Pohle, in the Catholic Encyclopedia, counts Ignatius (Smyrnaeans 7) among the 'most ancient Fathers' who 'attest without the slightest shadow of a misunderstanding' the Real Presence. Lutheran: the Missouri Synod's commemoration says Ignatius stressed 'the reality of Christ's bodily presence in the Lord's Supper'.

No Orthodox, Reformed, Anglican or Baptist document opened for this page discusses this verse. Each church's teaching on whether and how Christ is present in the Supper is set side by side in the card at Matthew 26:26.

a: It would be better for them to love
p: Greek agapan, 'to love', the verb of agape: perhaps a hint at the love feast of 8:2.
b: Greek synepheren de autois agapan, hina kai anastōsin. Lake: 'it were better for them to have love, that they also may attain to the Resurrection'. Ignatius has just said they 'do not care about love' (6:2). The same word family names the church's meal, the 'love feast', in 8:2.

a: to the prophets, and above all to the gospel
p: Ignatius's authorities: the prophets, and above all the gospel.
b: Greek tois prophētais, exairetōs de tō euangeliō. 'The gospel' here is the message of Christ's suffering and resurrection; whether Ignatius means a written Gospel is debated. Compare 5:1, where 'the prophecies', 'the law of Moses' and 'the gospel' fail to persuade the teachers.
orig: προσέχειν δὲ τοῖς προφήταις, ἐξαιρέτως δὲ τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ

a: Run from divisions
p: Greek merismos, 'division', kept apart from schisma, 'split'.
b: Greek tous merismous pheugete hōs archēn kakōn, 'flee divisions as the beginning of evils'. Merismos is a dividing into parts. The cure follows at once: 'follow the overseer' (8:1). Paul warned the Corinthians against 'splits' (1 Corinthians 1:10).

a: follow the overseer
p: Three offices: one overseer, a council of elders, and deacons.
b: Greek tō episkopō ... tō presbyteriō ... tous diakonous. Episkopos, 'overseer', is the word behind 'bishop'; presbyterion, 'council of elders', is the body of presbyters; diakonos is 'deacon'. The Plain English Translation uses the same words as its New Testament (Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:1-13). In the New Testament 'overseers' and 'elders' seem to name the same leaders (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7); in Ignatius one overseer leads each church, with the elders around him 'as if it were the apostles'. When and how the one overseer emerged, and whether it was meant to be permanent, are the questions on the cards at Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3.

a: Count that thanksgiving valid
p: Ignatius counts as valid the thanksgiving 'under the overseer, or under someone he entrusts it to'.
b: Greek ekeinē bebaia eucharistia hēgeisthō, hē hypo episkopon ousa ē hō an autos epitrepsē. Bebaia: Lightfoot, 'valid', as in Romans 4:16 and Hebrews 9:17; Lake also 'valid'. Lightfoot: 'This passage shows that the heretics celebrated the eucharist separately'. Ignatius does not say who the overseer's delegate would be (an elder is the obvious case), or what makes another meal invalid beyond its being apart from the overseer. The Catechism quotes this sentence (Catechism 1369). Who may lead the Supper today is the card on this chapter.

a: there is the catholic church
p: Greek he katholike ekklesia, 'the whole church': called by two church sources the first use of the phrase.
b:
Greek hē katholikē ekklēsia, from katholikos, 'whole, universal'. The Plain English Translation writes it lowercase: the word here is not yet the name of one communion. Lightfoot: here it is 'the general or universal Church, as opposed to a particular body of Christians', and later the phrase 'acquired a technical meaning ... as opposed to the heretical sects'. The comparison makes the point: as the people gather round their overseer in Smyrna, so the whole church gathers round Christ.

The Catholic Encyclopedia says that 'in Smyrnæans 8, we meet for the first time the phrase "Catholic Church"', and the Missouri Synod's commemoration that 'Ignatius was the first to use the word catholic to describe the universality of the Church'. The Catechism quotes this line, 'Where there is Christ Jesus, there is the Catholic Church' (Catechism 830).

a: to hold a love feast
p: Greek agapen poiein, 'to make an agape': a church meal, perhaps the thanksgiving itself.
b:
Greek oute baptizein oute agapēn poiein. Jude speaks of 'your love feasts' (Jude 1:12). Lake's footnote: 'Agapé means "love"; the name was given to some kind of religious meal. The context here suggests that it is a synonym for the Eucharist, but the point is doubted by some scholars.'

Lightfoot thinks the two were still one meal in Ignatius's day: in the apostles' time 'the eucharist formed part of the agape' (1 Corinthians 11:17-34), and 'the words οὔτε βαπτίζειν οὔτε ἀγάπην ποιεῖν seem to describe the two most important functions in which the bishop could bear a part, so that the ἀγάπη must include the eucharist'.

a: It is not lawful to baptize
p: Ignatius forbids baptism without the overseer; churches today differ on who may baptize.
b: Ignatius does not say what happens in an emergency or who besides the overseer may baptize with his approval. The Catholic Catechism today says the 'ordinary ministers' of baptism are 'the bishop and priest and, in the Latin Church, also the deacon', but 'In case of necessity, any person, even someone not baptized, can baptize, if he has the required intention' (Catechism 1256). The Westminster Confession says neither sacrament 'may be dispensed by any, but by a minister of the Word lawfully ordained' (27.4). See the card on this chapter and the baptism cards.

a: Whoever does anything behind the overseer's back is serving the devil
p: Greek lathra episkopou, 'secretly from the overseer'.
b: Greek ho lathra episkopou ti prassōn tō diabolō latreuei. Lake: 'without the knowledge of the bishop'. The point is secret meetings apart from the church's leader, the separate gatherings of 7:1-8:1. 'Serves' (latreuei) is a worship word: secret rites are worship given to the devil.
orig: ὁ λάθρα ἐπισκόπου τι πράσσων τῷ διαβόλῳ λατρεύει

a: Philo and Rheus Agathopus
p: Two companions who followed Ignatius from Syria: a deacon from Cilicia and 'an elect man'.
b: Ignatius's letter To the Philadelphians (chapter 11) calls Philo 'the deacon from Cilicia' and Rheus Agathopus 'an elect man who is following me from Syria' (Lake's English). The Catholic Encyclopedia says the 'Martyrium Ignatii' is 'reputed to have been written by Philo, deacon of Tarsus, and Rheus Agathopus', and that they carried his relics back to Antioch; that account is late and, the article says, 'greatly interpolated'. For the name 'Rheus', see the variant.

a: a life in exchange for yours
p: Greek antipsychon: Ignatius offers his life and chains for the Smyrnaeans.
b: Greek antipsychon hymōn to pneuma mou kai ta desma mou, 'a life-for-life of you, my spirit and my chains'. 4 Maccabees uses the word of the martyrs' deaths for Israel (4 Maccabees 6:29; 4 Maccabees 17:21). Lake: 'May my spirit be for your life'.

a: which you did not look down on and were not ashamed of
p: Lake's margin gives 2 Timothy 1:16, Onesiphorus.
b: Paul blesses Onesiphorus, 'because many times he lifted my spirits, and my chain did not shame him' (2 Timothy 1:16). Ignatius echoes it and turns it: since they were not ashamed of his chains, Christ will not be ashamed of them (compare Mark 8:38).

a: Your prayer has gone out to the church in Antioch
p: News has come that the church at Antioch is at peace again.
b: Ignatius learned at Troas that the trouble at Antioch was over (11:2, 'they are at peace'). The letter does not say what the trouble had been, persecution or division. The Orthodox Church in America's life says that at Troas 'he heard the happy news of the end of the persecution against Christians in Antioch'. Lake counts among Ignatius's aims his wish 'to secure the future of his own church in Antioch by persuading other communities to send helpers'.

a: not from anything in my own conscience
p: Greek ouk ek syneidotos: not because he has a clear conscience of deserving it.
b: Greek ouk ek syneidotos all' ek charitos theou. Lake: 'not that I am conscious of deserts', with the footnote 'Or, possibly, "by my own complicity"'. Paul: 'I am aware of nothing against myself, but I am not justified by that' (1 Corinthians 4:4), and 'It is by God's grace that I am what I am' (1 Corinthians 15:10).
orig: οὐκ ἐκ συνειδότος ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ χάριτος θεοῦ

a: elect an envoy of God
p: Greek theopresbeutes, 'God-ambassador', elected by the church.
b: Greek cheirotonēsai ... theopresbeutēn. Cheirotoneō first meant to vote by raising the hand; here the church elects its delegate (as in 2 Corinthians 8:19, where 'the churches voted for him'). Theopresbeutēs, 'ambassador of God', is a rare compound. Lightfoot prints the form θεοπρεσβύτης, says 'There can be no doubt about the meaning of the word', and notes that the forms presbeutēs and presbytēs were confused at this time. In his letter To Polycarp (chapter 7) the same messenger is called theodromos, 'God's runner'.

a: their own body has been restored to them
p: Greek somateion, 'body, corporation': the church's life as a body.
b: Greek apekatestathē autois to idion sōmateion. Sōmateion was used of a corporate body, a guild or society. Lake: 'their proper constitution has been restored'. The church at Antioch is whole again.

a: You are mature, so think mature thoughts as well
p: Lake's margin gives Philippians 3:15.
b: Greek teleioi ontes teleia kai phroneite. Paul: 'So let those of us who are mature think this way' (Philippians 3:15). Teleios is 'perfect, complete, mature': Ignatius uses it four times in 11:1-3 ('in full', 'complete', and twice here); it is the word rendered 'perfect' in 4:2 and 10:2. Here the Plain English Translation uses 'mature' so that the echo of the site's Philippians 3:15 stays visible.

a: Troas
p: Ignatius wrote this letter at Troas, the port where Paul saw the man of Macedonia.
b: Eusebius: 'when he was already past Smyrna, from Troas he again addressed in writing those in Philadelphia, and the church of the Smyrnaeans, and in particular Polycarp, who led it' (Church History 3.36.10, the site's translation of the Greek). Troas, on the coast of Asia facing Macedonia, was where Paul had his vision of the man of Macedonia (Acts 16:8-11) and where he broke bread with the believers on the first day of the week (Acts 20:6-12).

a: Burrhus
p: A deacon of Ephesus who acted as Ignatius's writer or carrier.
b: In his letter to the Ephesians Ignatius calls Burrhus 'my fellow slave ... your deacon' and asks that he stay with him (Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1). 'By Burrhus' means by his hand: as writer or as carrier. Lake's footnote: the spelling 'varies considerably' in the manuscripts, and 'It is possible that Βόρρος, which has some support in L is really right.'

a: your overseer, worthy of God
p: Ignatius greets Smyrna's overseer without naming him; elsewhere it is Polycarp.
b: Greek ton axiotheon episkopon. The letter never names him. Ignatius's separate letter To Polycarp is addressed to 'Polycarp, overseer of the church of the Smyrnaeans' (Lake's text of its greeting), and Eusebius calls Polycarp the one 'who led it' (Church History 3.36.10, the site's translation of the Greek). The overseer, the council of elders and the deacons are greeted in that order, the three offices of 8:1.

a: the virgins who are called widows
p: A puzzling phrase: virgins in the order of widows, or widows so pure they are called virgins?
b: Greek tas parthenous tas legomenas chēras. The church had an enrolled order of widows (1 Timothy 5:3-16; Polycarp to the Philippians 4:3). The phrase, Lightfoot says, 'is generally explained' as meaning that the order of widows included, or was made up of, unmarried virgins; he names Cotelier, Hefele and others who also identified the widows with the deaconesses. Lightfoot objected: Paul's rules require real widows over sixty (1 Timothy 5:9), and Tertullian calls 'a virgin widow' a 'monstrum'. He proposed instead: 'I salute those women whom, though by name and in outward condition they are widows, I prefer to call virgins, for such they are in God's sight by their purity and devotion.'
r: 1 Timothy 5:3-16; Acts 6:1; Acts 9:39-41; Polycarp to the Philippians 4:3

a: the household of Tavia
p: A woman who led a household church; the Armenian and long recension read 'Gavia'.
b: Ignatius greets 'the household of Tavia' and prays for her faith, as for the head of a house church (compare Nympha, Colossians 4:15, and Lydia, Acts 16:15). Lightfoot preferred the form Gavia: 'The names Gavius, Gavia, are frequent in the Latin inscriptions', while he had 'not observed any example of Tavia'. See the variant.

a: Alce
p: Greeted again in the letter To Polycarp, and perhaps the Alce of the Martyrdom of Polycarp.
b: Lightfoot: Alce is greeted in the same words, 'a name dear to me', in the companion letter To Polycarp (chapter 8), and the name appears in the Martyrdom of Polycarp, where Nicetes is 'Herod's father and the brother of Alce' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 17:2). He sees 'no difficulty, though a period of forty or fifty years may have elapsed, in supposing the same person to be meant', a family divided over Christ, as in Matthew 10:35.
